Task result written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Output evaluation written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Task quality check written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Ticket resolution written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Contract review written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Patch review written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Regression review written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Fact check written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Content verification written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Text authenticity review written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
Ai text assessment written by a language model. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.

Whether an image is authentic, edited or AI-generated. It reads the file's own metadata first (C2PA manifest, IPTC digital source type, generator parameters, editing software, camera), then a vision model reports only visible signs. A firm verdict needs metadata or a visible generator mark; otherwise it is Likely or Inconclusive. Images only, up to 5 MB.

Forensic check of an image: embedded metadata (C2PA, IPTC digital source type, generator parameters, editing software, camera) and visible signs of editing, with findings and a verdict. A firm verdict needs metadata or a visible generator mark. Images only, up to 5 MB.

Caption of an image by a vision model: what it shows, the main objects and any legible text. It describes only what is visible and names no person or place unless written in the image. Images only, up to 5 MB.

Whether a US airport, or either end of a route between US airports, is disrupted now, from the FAA National Airspace System status: ground stops, ground delay programs, arrival and departure delays and closures, with the delay in minutes. Airports outside the US and bare flight numbers are reported as not covered.

Smart contract security review written by a language model: findings with the function, why each is exploitable and the fix, and the worst severity. It reviews the source code given and asks for source when only an address is sent. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.

Invoice and ledger reconciliation written by a language model: whether they match, the discrepancy (ledger minus invoice) and each mismatch with both figures. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.

Document authenticity assessment written by a language model from the text alone: impossible dates, arithmetic, identifier formats and issuer wording, with a verdict and the evidence. No register or issuer is contacted. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.

Plagiarism check written by a language model against sources retrieved for the request: a verdict, the share of matching text and each match with its source. Any answer that judges something the model did not measure says so, and sources are only those retrieved for the request.
A real text embedding from Google's gemini-embedding-001 at 768 dimensions, L2-normalised: the whole vector, its dimension, the norm before normalisation and the exact text embedded.

What a recent satellite image shows at a place: NASA GIBS MODIS Terra true-colour imagery (about 250 m per pixel) for the date asked or the latest full day, read by a vision model for cloud, smoke, snow, water, burn scars and land cover, with the capture date and image link. Features under a few hundred metres are stated as not visible.

Whether a social account behaves like a bot, from its public profile on Bluesky, Mastodon or GitHub: self-declared bot flags, account age, posting rate, follow ratios, empty profiles and handle patterns, with a bot score and the signals. X, Instagram and TikTok have no keyless profile source and are reported as inconclusive.

A wash-trading screen for a token or pair from DEX Screener live data on its busiest pool: turnover against liquidity, buy and sell balance, trade size and pool age, with an estimated wash share only when two independent signs agree. Exchanges get their CoinGecko trust score; NFT collections are not covered.

A service's uptime over a period from the incidents on its public Statuspage (major outages in full, partial outages at 30%), against the SLA target stated, the provider's published SLA or 99.9%, with whether it complied and the downtime minutes.

Product authenticity assessment written by a language model from the description given: price against retail, seller and shipping red flags, model numbers, packaging and sales channel, with a verdict and the evidence. The item, seller and brand are not checked, and every answer says so.

Shipment delay risk written by a language model from the details given and general route knowledge: chokepoints, seasonal peaks, weather seasons, customs and carrier reliability, with a risk level, a delay probability and the factors. No live tracking, port or weather data is read, and every answer says so.

Whether a video is authentic, edited or AI-generated. It reads the file's container metadata first (C2PA manifest, generator and editor tags, encoder, camera), then a vision model reports only visible signs in clips up to 8 MB. A firm verdict needs metadata or a visible generator mark; YouTube links are judged from their thumbnail frame only, at most Inconclusive.

Transcript of the speech in an audio file at a public URL (MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC or M4A, up to 8 MB), written by a speech-capable model in the original language with the detected language. Nothing is transcribed without audio.

Whether a carrier (USPS, UPS, FedEx, DHL, Aramex, Canada Post, Purolator, Royal Mail, Evri, Deutsche Post, La Poste, PostNL, Australia Post, Japan Post, India Post, Blue Dart, Delhivery, OnTrac) delivers to an area, at country level: the postal code is checked against a public postal-code database, and the carrier's home market and announced suspensions decide, with the services offered. Address-level remoteness needs the carrier's own lookup, and every answer says so.

Checks that a purchase happened as claimed by comparing the order, receipt, payment and delivery details given: order number, merchant, items, amounts, tax, total and payment status, with the arithmetic shown. A language model does the comparison; the merchant's order system is not accessed, and an order number alone is reported as unverified.

Checks a purchase order against the invoice, delivery note or receipt given (a three-way match when all are present): line items, quantities ordered and delivered, unit prices, totals and currency, listing each mismatch with both figures. A language model does the comparison; no procurement or vendor system is accessed, and a PO number alone is reported as unverified.

Change, cancellation and refund rules for an airline fare (carrier, fare brand, fare basis or booking class), with any claim checked against them: refundable or not, the change fee, and each rule. Uses fare rules quoted in the request, else the carrier's published fare families as a language model knows them; the ticket's live fare rules are not retrieved, and every answer says so.

Delivery window in business days for a carrier service between two places, from the carrier's published service standards (zone-based ground transit, overnight and two-day commitments) as a language model knows them, marked as an estimate unless the service carries a published guarantee. No live tracking or carrier transit calculator is used.

Estimated shipping price and transit days for a parcel of a given weight between two places, for the most common economical tracked service on that lane, with a likely price range and what changes it. An estimate from published retail rate tables as a language model knows them, not a carrier quote; every answer says so.

Open ports, exposed services and fingerprint-matched CVEs for a host (IPv4 address, domain or URL), from Shodan InternetDB, the public index of Shodan's internet-wide scans. Passive: no connection is made to the host, so the answer is Shodan's latest observation (about weekly), and it says so. Ports that should rarely face the internet (Telnet, SMB, RDP, databases, Redis, Docker API) are flagged and set the risk level.

Text to speech: the given text spoken by a Gemini speech model, returned as a 16-bit mono WAV clip in base64 (audio_base64) with its duration, sample rate, voice and model. Up to 1,200 characters per clip; longer text is cut at a sentence end and the answer says so. Voices: Kore (default), Puck, Charon, Fenrir, Aoede, Leda, Orus, Zephyr.

A retailer's standard return window in days, with its main conditions and exceptions, read from the retailer's own return-policy page when it answers a plain request (verified: true, with the page as the source). Retailers whose pages refuse automated clients get the commonly published window, marked verified: false.

Live AIS telemetry for a vessel named by MMSI, IMO number or name, from Fintraffic Digitraffic's open AIS feed (Finnish waters and much of the northern Baltic): position, speed over ground, course, heading, navigational status, draught, destination and ETA, with the position's age. AIS carries no fuel burn, so none is reported.

Live congestion at a Finnish port (Helsinki, Turku, Kotka, Hamina, Rauma, Oulu and others, or its UN/LOCODE) from Fintraffic Digitraffic's port-call register and AIS: vessels at berth, expected in 24 hours and departed in 24 hours, vessels waiting at anchor nearby, average arrival delay against ETA and berth dwell time, with a low/moderate/high level. Ports outside Finland are reported as not covered.

Recent public social posts about a topic or #hashtag from Bluesky's public search, Mastodon's public hashtag timeline and Hacker News, each with platform, author, time and link. X (Twitter) has no search without a paid API key, and the answer says it was not searched.

A product's current price: from a store's own public Shopify product feed when a product link is given (live price and availability per variant), otherwise the latest dated shelf prices photographed in shops on Open Prices (prices.openfoodfacts.org) for a product named or given by barcode. Marketplaces that refuse automated clients are not fetched.

Whether a product, or one size or variant of it, is in stock right now, read from the store's own public Shopify product feed for the product link given, with every variant's availability, price and SKU. Without a store link there is no open live-inventory source, and the answer says so instead of guessing.

The open-data part of a KYC check: the applicant's name screened against the OFAC SDN, OFAC consolidated and UN Security Council sanctions lists, including names asked without their middle names. Biometric liveness, selfie-to-ID matching and document authenticity need a live capture session and the document, so they are reported as not performed, never as passed.

Cloud utilization graded from the readings in the request (CPU, memory, disk, GPU, network as % or used/total) against common alerting thresholds, and a named provider's live public health from its own status feed: AWS Health, Google Cloud Service Health, Azure status, or the Statuspage of GitHub, Cloudflare, DigitalOcean, Vercel and others. An account's private metrics are never claimed.

Whether a sensor is alive and reporting sane values: public sensors read live by id (USGS water gauges, Sensor.Community, NWS/ASOS stations such as KSEA), with heartbeat freshness against the asked interval and each value checked against its physical range; readings pasted into the request are graded from that data only.

A credit profile given in the request graded against published benchmarks: the score placed in the FICO or VantageScore band (and checked for the 300-850 range), debt-to-income (stated, or from monthly debts and income) against the 36% preferred, 43% Qualified Mortgage and 50% automated-underwriting limits, revolving utilization against the advised 30%, and stated adverse factors. No credit bureau is queried.

Datacenter readings given in the request graded against published benchmarks: PUE against the Uptime Institute industry average, inlet temperature and humidity against the ASHRAE recommended and class A1 allowable envelopes, and backup generator fuel level and days since its last load test against NFPA 110. A facility's own telemetry is never claimed.

Stock counts given in the request worked through: units available after allocations, days of cover at the stated demand, the reorder point (stated, or demand x lead time + safety stock) and whether a replenishment order is due or the item is stocked out. A warehouse system's own records are never claimed.

input_schema.description: Each endpoint reads the one parameter it needs. Parameters are matched tolerantly: a hostname, URL, address or transaction hash is also recovered from a free-text question, so router-supplied phrasing still resolves.

asset.description: Cryptocurrency ticker or name. Used by /crypto-price.

block.description: Block number to read at. Used by /token-supply and /onchain-metric.

chain.description: EVM chain name or alias — ethereum, base, arbitrum, optimism, polygon, sepolia, base-sepolia. Defaults to ethereum. Used by the on-chain endpoints.

cve_query.description: The complete CVE_LOOKUP question for /cve, including the CVE identifier and every requested fact. Preserve the question verbatim rather than reducing it to the identifier.

domain.description: Hostname, HTTPS URL, or host:port. Used by /ssl-check and /dns.

ip.description: IPv4 or IPv6 address to locate. Used by /ip-geolocation.

pair.description: Currency pair or a question naming two currencies, as ISO 4217 codes or common names. Used by /fx-rate.

protocol.description: DeFi protocol or chain name. Used by /tvl.

query.description: The full question, verbatim. Accepted by every endpoint.

symbol.description: Equity ticker or company name. Used by /stock-price.

token.description: Token symbol or 0x contract address. Used by /token-supply.

topic.description: The complete ACADEMIC_SEARCH question for /papers, including the research subject and any publication dates, result count, field constraints or requested ordering. Preserve the question verbatim rather than reducing it to keywords.

type.description: DNS record type or types, comma-separated. Used by /dns.

url.description: Absolute URL to scan. Used by /url-scan; a free-text URL_SCAN question may instead name one of the documented historical incidents.

output_schema.description: Every endpoint returns verdict, confidence and reason, so one signal mapping covers all intents. The remaining fields are those of the endpoint that was called.

verdict.description: Primary decision. /ssl-check returns a certificate verdict, /url-scan a safety verdict, /gas-price a congestion level, /wallet-balance funded or empty, /tx-lookup a transaction status, /tvl the kind of subject resolved, /crypto-price whether a quote was found. "unavailable" means an upstream source did not answer, which is distinct from the subject not existing.

body.name: LiveCert — Sourced Answers for Agents
body.description: Sourced answers for agents and apps across 42 intents, each read live from a named primary source so the caller can check it. Every answer opens with a one-sentence answer, then returns the values as fields, the source and the time it was checked. Compliance: sanctions screening of people, companies and wallets against the OFAC SDN and UN lists with near-match scores; company register records (status, company number, register, registered address and agent, parents) from GLEIF and SEC EDGAR; SEC filings with acceptance times and each 10-Q or 10-K's own XBRL figures; URL reputation from Cloudflare and Quad9 threat DNS, each source named. Research: question answering with every claim cited, web search with dated reports, fact checks with the source URL and evidence sentence, and academic, clinical and news search. Markets: prices and market data for coins, tokens and listed companies, 10-K revenue and earnings, exchange rates and macroeconomic prints (US CPI and unemployment from BLS, the federal funds target range from the New York Fed, euro-area HICP from Eurostat and ECB rates). On-chain: transfer verification with confirmations and the burned base fee, transaction and contract activity across EVM chains, wallet balances, gas, token holders, ERC-20 total supply and burned balance read at a pinned block from two RPCs, any named value read at a stated block height (receipt gas and Transfer amounts, storage slots, balances, block gas), and cross-chain messages. Security: live TLS certificates, URL scans, CVE records, DNS records compared across two resolvers, and fraud signals. Weather: forecasts, current conditions and storm risk. Also translation, IP geolocation, prediction market outcomes, text extraction, sentiment and classification. Chat replies, code reviews and requested writing are generated by a language model (Groq gpt-oss-120b, with two fallbacks), each field checked before it is served and an honest unknown when no model answers; the question-answering, sentiment and classification sentences are phrased by a model with a keyless fallback, and a phrased answer is kept only when every claim cites a numbered source; everything else is computed, not generated.

endpoints.description: Example questions: "Is the TLS certificate for github.com valid?", "When does example.com's certificate expire?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and domain, valid, chain_complete, issuer, valid_to, days_remaining. Live TLS certificate check for one domain. Accepts a bare hostname, a full URL, or host:port.

Example questions: "Is there a storm risk in Chennai in the next 48 hours?", "Will gusts exceed 60 km/h in Miami tonight?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and location, risk_score, wind_direction, max_wind_gust_kmh, max_wind_speed_kmh, max_precipitation_mm, thunderstorm, window_hours, valid_at, peak_at, latitude, longitude, threshold_exceeded, threshold_hours. Severe-weather risk for a location over the next 48 hours. Accepts a place name or "lat,lon".

Example questions: "Find recent peer-reviewed papers on CRISPR gene editing", "Most cited papers on transformer models since 2023". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and topic, from_date, to_date, papers, count. Finds peer-reviewed papers on a topic, optionally within a date range, via OpenAlex. Returns title, authors, year and citation count for each.

Example questions: "Translate 'Good morning' into French", "Say hello in Spanish". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and source_text, target_language, target_code, translation, source. Translates quoted text into a named target language. Returns the translation itself, in the target script.

Example questions: "Where is 8.8.8.8 located?", "Which network owns 1.1.1.1?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and ip, city, region, country, country_code, latitude, longitude, timezone, asn, organisation. Live IP geolocation. Accepts an IPv4 or IPv6 address, or a whole question containing one.

Example questions: "What is the forecast for London tomorrow?", "What is the weather in Tokyo right now?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and location, window_hours, span_days, start_time, end_time, hourly_count, temp_min_c, temp_max_c, total_precipitation_mm, precipitation_probability_max_pct, max_wind_speed_kmh, precipitation_hours, latitude, longitude. Current and future conditions for a location. hours=0 reports the present hour; any other value gives a window of up to 168h, and the default with no hours parameter is 24h. Accepts a place name or "lat,lon".

Example questions: "Extract the dates and amounts from this invoice: …". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and extracted. Structured extraction from text supplied inline in the question. Reads quantities and units, contact details, named entities, action items, dates and events, or bare numeric values, and answers with the extracted fields themselves. The text is carried in the question, so nothing is fetched and the answer is deterministic and checkable against the input.

Example questions: "What are today's technology headlines?", "Top business news in Europe". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and topic, region, headlines, count. Current news headlines for a topic and optional region, read live from Google News at request time and returned as a numbered list with each source named. Honours a requested count such as "top 5". Headlines rotate, so the answer states the date it was read.

Example questions: "What is the ETH balance of vitalik.eth?", "Balance of 0x… on Base". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and address, chain, balance_eth, symbol. Native-coin balance of an EVM address, read with eth_getBalance at the latest block from public JSON-RPC on the chain the question names — Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism or Polygon. A zero balance is reported as zero; an RPC that does not answer is reported as unavailable rather than as zero. Token balances such as USDT are not included, and the answer says so when one was asked about.

On-chain activity, asked about a transaction or about an address. Example questions: "Did transaction 0x… succeed, and who sent it to whom?", "When was contract 0x… deployed and how many transactions does it have?". For a transaction it returns verdict and a transaction object with status, from, to, value_wei, value, symbol, block_number, block_hash, receipt_status, method, gas_used, fee_wei, confirmations, base_fee_wei and base_fee_burned, which is true on Ethereum and Polygon, where the EIP-1559 base fee is burned, and false on rollups, where it is paid to the sequencer. A transaction is read by hash from public JSON-RPC on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, BNB Chain or Avalanche; where no chain is named every one of them is searched rather than one being assumed. It reports confirmed, reverted, pending or not found, with the sender and recipient, value moved, total fee, the base fee and whether it was burned, confirmations, gas used, block number, any contract deployed and the count of ERC-20 transfers in the receipt. An address is answered from the chain and its block explorer on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism or Polygon: whether it is a contract, an externally owned account, or an account carrying an EIP-7702 delegation; when a contract was deployed; how many transactions are recorded against it; how many an account has sent; and when it was last active, where a recency read the index could not date is reported as undated rather than as inactive. On Ethereum an explorer outage fails over to a second index whose count is attributed and may trail the chain. A reverted transaction is reported as reverted, not as a failure to answer; an RPC or explorer that does not respond is reported as unknown rather than as not found, because those are different facts; and a chain this endpoint does not read is named as unsupported rather than answered from a different chain.

Example questions: "What is the severity and affected versions of CVE-2021-44228?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and cve_id, severity, cvss_score, cvss_version, scored_by, affected_product, affected_versions, other_products_affected, cwe, status, published, description, source, source_url. Vulnerabilities from the National Vulnerability Database, asked three ways. By CVE identifier: the severity rating and CVSS base score with the CVSS version and the source that assigned it, the affected product and versions resolved from the record's CPE configuration — exact versions and half-open ranges alike — and what the flaw is. By year or severity, such as "critical CVEs 2025" or "latest CVEs": the vulnerabilities published in a stated window of at most 120 days with the highest-scored named, where a severity band is applied to each record's own CVSS base score rather than to the database's severity flag. By product and vulnerability class, such as "Forgejo remote code execution": the matching record and the fixed release where one is documented, used only when the record names the product asked about. A record with no CVSS score yet is reported as unscored rather than given an invented severity; a REJECTED identifier is reported as rejected rather than as not found; a truncated identifier is named as incomplete; and a rate-limited or unreachable database is reported as unknown, never as a vulnerability that does not exist.

Example questions: "Latest news about the EU AI Act", "What happened with Boeing this week?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and subject, window_days, articles, count. News article coverage of a topic, entity or time period, searched rather than browsed. Returns individual articles — each with its headline, the publisher that ran it and its publication date, most relevant first — for a subject read from the question, over a window the question may state ("in the last 3 days", "this month"). A recency word with no explicit window is treated as a request rather than a filter: the last 30 days are searched first and the search is widened only if nothing on the subject was published in them, and the answer says when that happened. Articles that are not about the subject are dropped rather than used as padding, with the acronym of a named entity counted as naming it. This is article coverage; a plain list of current headlines is /headlines. A news index that does not respond is reported as unknown, never as an absence of coverage.

Example questions: "Convert 100 USD to EUR", "What is 5,000 yen in dollars?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and from, to, amount, rate, converted, kind, as_of. An exchange rate, or an amount converted between two currencies. The primary source is the European Central Bank's euro foreign exchange reference rate, which is published once per day and therefore does not move between reads; the answer states that it is a reference rate and the date it was published for, so it is never mistaken for a live trading quote. The rate is given in both directions and the conversion direction is taken from the question, including the "how many X is Y" phrasing that names the target first. Currencies the ECB does not publish fall back to a market rate, and that answer says it is a market rate instead. A request naming only one currency is refused rather than half-answered, and a source that does not respond is reported as unknown rather than as a rate of zero.

Example questions: "What is the gas price on Ethereum right now?", "Gas on Base in Gwei". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and chain, gwei, base_fee_gwei, priority_gwei, block. The current transaction fee level on a named chain, read from that chain's own JSON-RPC. Reports the gas price in Gwei both exactly and rounded, the base fee and priority fee that make it up, the block the reading is from so the figure is checkable, and what a standard 21,000-gas transfer costs at that rate. This is the fee level and never the chain token's price, which is a different intent. Covers the mainnets ethereum, base, arbitrum, optimism, polygon, bsc (BNB Smart Chain) and avalanche (C-Chain); a chain outside that list, or a test network such as Sepolia or Holesky, is named as uncovered rather than answered with a mainnet's fee, and an unresponsive endpoint is reported as unknown rather than as a fee of zero.

Example questions: "What is Solana's market cap and 24-hour volume?", "Apple's revenue and P/E from its 10-K". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and subject, name, chain, data. Market data and financial statistics for a coin, a token or a listed company, deliberately beyond a single quoted price. A coin named in words, such as Solana or Bitcoin, returns market capitalisation, 24-hour trading volume in dollars, fully diluted valuation, 24-hour range and change. A token contract address with its chain returns market capitalisation, 24-hour trading volume, fully diluted valuation and last traded price. A ticker or company name returns the day range, share volume, 52-week range and change against the previous close, with the ticker resolved from the company name where only a name is given. Revenue, net income and earnings per share come from the company's latest 10-K, and a price-to-earnings ratio is computed from the last traded price and the 10-K's diluted earnings per share, with both inputs named. A figure that could not be retrieved, such as margins, is stated as not retrieved rather than substituted.

Example questions: "Is 0x… a scam address?", "This email asks me to pay an invoice in gift cards: is it fraud?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and subject, evidence, not_checked, sanctioned, flagged_hosts, scam_markers. How likely a named address, link or message is to be fraudulent, assessed from checks that are actually performed and named in the answer: the OFAC sanctioned digital-currency address listing, Cloudflare's threat-intelligence resolver for any domain in the text, the address's own on-chain state (contract, externally owned account, or an account carrying an EIP-7702 delegation, with its transaction count and balance), and specific scam wording such as a request for a seed phrase, gift-card payment or changed banking details. A sanctions hit or a domain blocked as malware is reported as high risk. A clean result is reported as no indicators found among the checks performed, with the checks listed, and explicitly not as a statement that the subject is safe; a check that could not be completed is named as such rather than counted as clean. An academic paper named by title is checked against OpenAlex's retraction record, and a retraction is reported as high risk. No keyless source records misconduct findings, paper-mill membership or predatory-publisher status, so the answer names those three as not checked rather than implying a clean record, and a title that cannot be matched to one indexed work is reported as not found rather than matched loosely to a similar one.

Example questions: "How many holders does USDC have on Ethereum?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and symbol, name, address, chain, holders, top_holder_percent. How many distinct addresses hold a named ERC-20 token, read from the chain's own transfer index via Blockscout. The token may be given as a contract address or as a symbol together with its chain, and where no chain is named every supported chain is checked rather than one being assumed, because the same symbol carries different holder counts on different chains. The answer names the contract the figure came from so it is checkable. Where the question also asks about concentration, the share of supply held by the single largest holder is reported, and where that list does not return in time the answer says so rather than omitting it silently. This is a headcount of holders and never a balance, a price, a supply figure or pool liquidity, each of which is a different intent. An identifier that is not a token, such as a CVE number, is named as such rather than searched for. Where more than one token on a chain shares a symbol with no dominant one among them, a contract address is asked for instead of one being picked. Covers ethereum, base, arbitrum, optimism and polygon.

Example questions: "What clinical trials are testing semaglutide for Alzheimer's?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and subject, trials, citations. An answer to one research question, drawn from named sources: the ClinicalTrials.gov registry for trial phase, status and completion dates, Europe PMC for published literature, and Wikipedia for subjects that are neither. Every source is cited by identifier — the NCT number of a trial, the title, first author and year of a paper — so the answer can be checked rather than taken on trust, and a source is only cited when it actually names the subject asked about. Where the question asks about an outcome that has not been decided, such as whether a drug will be approved, the registered evidence to date is reported and the answer states plainly that no decision has been recorded; no outcome is predicted. Where neither index holds anything on the subject that is what the answer says, named as an absence in those indexes rather than as an absence of research. A request to combine findings across many sources into a synthesis is the RESEARCH_SYNTHESIS intent rather than this one.

Example questions: "What is the price of ETH?", "BTC price in EUR on 2025-01-01". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and asset, symbol, price, quote, price_at, source, aggregate_price. The current or historical price of one named cryptocurrency, as a single quoted figure with the venue that quoted it and the UTC time of the quote. The current price is the last Coinbase trade where Coinbase lists the pair, Kraken's last trade where it does not, and CoinGecko's cross-venue aggregate as a cross-check or fallback; the answer says it is a live quote that moves between reads. The quote currency follows the question (USD by default; EUR, GBP, JPY, INR and other major fiat, or BTC and ETH). A dollar stablecoin's answer also states its distance from the one-dollar peg. A date returns that UTC day's Coinbase open and close and CoinGecko's daily snapshot, labelled as historical. This is one price, never market capitalisation or volume, which is FINANCIAL_DATA, and never what an address holds, which is WALLET_BALANCE_CHECK. A fork or wrapped asset such as Bitcoin Cash, Ethereum Classic or Wrapped Bitcoin is priced as itself, never as the major whose name it contains, and a multi-word coin name is matched whole. Testnet assets are answered as having no market price, a future date is declined as a prediction, an asset name that matches no listed coin exactly is not substituted with a similar one, and a provider outage is reported as an outage rather than a missing price.

Example questions: "What is Apple's share price?", "TSLA closing price on 2026-09-01". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and ticker, name, price, currency, price_at, exchange, market_open, source. The current or historical share price of one listed equity, given as a ticker or a company name. Every answer states the exchange, the quote time in the exchange's own time zone, and whether the regular trading session is open right now; outside the session the figure is labelled as the last session price and never presented as a live quote. A company name is resolved to its ticker and accepted only when the listing carries every word of the name asked about, so an unlisted subsidiary is answered as not found rather than with a related company's price. A ticker is read only when it is written as one in capitals, and a currency code such as (USD) is never taken for a ticker. A question that does not ask about a share price, such as a weather question naming a city, is refused rather than priced. An ISO date returns that day's closing price, and a date with no session is said to have none. A question asking whether a stock will rise or fall is answered with the price and an explicit statement that no forecast is made. Company fundamentals and statistics beyond one price are FINANCIAL_DATA. A provider outage, including a failed ticker search, is reported as an outage and never as the company not being listed.

Example questions: "Was LayerZero message 0x… delivered from Ethereum to Arbitrum?", "Did bridge transaction 0x… arrive on Base?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and message (guid, nonce, source_chain, destination_chain, sender, receiver, source_tx, destination_tx, scan_status). Whether a LayerZero V2 bridge message sent from one chain was executed on another, verified from both chains' own receipts rather than taken from an indexer's status. The message is located on LayerZero Scan by its source or destination transaction hash or its GUID; the source receipt must carry the endpoint's PacketSent event and the destination receipt its PacketDelivered event, and both must agree on nonce, sender, receiver and GUID. Answers are verified, not yet delivered, mismatch (including a message that travels between different chains than the ones asked about), or not found. Covers ethereum, base, arbitrum, optimism, polygon, bsc and avalanche. State roots, Merkle-Patricia proofs and block headers are not verified cryptographically, and every answer to a request for one says so. Other bridges such as Wormhole or native rollup bridges are not checked. A nonce with no transaction hash, GUID or sender does not identify a message, and one is asked for. An RPC or indexer outage is reported as an outage.

Example questions: "Who won the 2024 US presidential election?", "Has the Polymarket market on … resolved?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and outcome, winner, event, source. The actual outcome of a named, checkable event, as settled by a public prediction market, for a market or conditional contract to resolve against. Polymarket's real-money markets and Manifold's play-money markets are searched, and a market is used only when it carries every name and number in the question, asks about the same move (a cut, a rise or no change), and is mostly about that event, so a market on a different subject or the opposite proposition that shares most of the words is not used. A settled market is reported with its settled outcome and the market's own wording, and a Manifold settlement is labelled as play money. An unsettled market is reported as unresolved with its scheduled close, and its trading odds are never given as an outcome. Nothing is predicted: a request for an opinion or forecast is declined by name, and a question that names no specific event is asked to name one. Where no matching market exists the answer says so; official sources such as flight trackers, election authorities and league results are not read. A provider outage is reported as an outage.

Example questions: "Is https://example.com/offer safe to click?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and url, flagged_by, checks. A safe or unsafe verdict on one URL, with the evidence behind it named. The host is resolved through Cloudflare's malware-and-phishing filtering resolver and compared with an unfiltered resolver, so a block is reported only when the filter answers 0.0.0.0 for a name that really resolves; Quad9 threat-blocking DNS is compared with its unfiltered resolver the same way; the TLS certificate is inspected; and the redirect chain is walked hop by hop, each hop checked to be a public address before it is contacted. A listing makes a URL unsafe. A brand name used on a domain that is not a known domain of that brand, punycode, a bare IP address or an invalid certificate makes it suspicious. With none of those, and only when both threat-filtering resolvers answered, the URL is reported as appearing safe, and the answer says plainly that no blocklist can prove a site safe. A host that does not resolve is reported as unreachable. When either threat source does not answer, that is reported as an outage and never as a safe verdict. A question only about a certificate is SSL_VERIFICATION and is refused by name, and a list of which engines flag a URL is URL_SAFE.

Example questions: "What is the latest news on the Fed's rate decision?", "Who is the CEO of OpenAI?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and articles, background. Current, externally sourced information for a question that static knowledge cannot answer, taken from Google News search and, when no current report exists, from Wikipedia. The answer quotes the most relevant reports' headlines with publisher and publication date, so every clause can be checked; nothing is paraphrased by a model. A report is only cited when it names the subject, and when the question names a product or trial code such as MK-2870 the headline must name that code. A question about a future outcome is answered with the current coverage and states that it is not a prediction. A TLS certificate check, a scholarly literature search, a single CVE record or a request to explain a concept from static knowledge is refused by name as the intent it belongs to. When the sources that answered find nothing on the subject, that is reported as an absence in those sources only; when Google News does not answer, that is reported as an outage.

Example questions: "What is the sentiment of this review: 'The product broke after one day'?". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and compound, positive_words, negative_words, tones. The sentiment a supplied text expresses — positive, negative, neutral or mixed — read by a hosted open-weight language model called over the network, which writes the label and a short explanation. When that model does not answer within its time budget the text is read instead with a rule-based word list and the VADER method (negation, intensifiers, a contrastive "but", capitals and exclamation marks), and everything below describes that fallback. A negation reaches at most three words forward and never across a comma or full stop, so "No problems, great service" reads as positive. The answer names the words that carried the label, so it can be checked against the text, and names an emotional tone such as frustrated or joyful only when a word in the text states it and is not negated. A text with no opinion word is reported as neutral with that reason given. Sarcasm, irony and opinion words outside the list are not detected, so a neutral reading can be a miss. Assigning a text to caller-supplied categories is TEXT_CLASSIFICATION rather than this intent. A request with no text is refused by name rather than scored.

Example questions: "Classify this ticket as billing, technical or account: 'I was charged twice'". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and label. Assigns a supplied text to one of the labels the request itself supplies, such as billing, technical or account issue. There is no fixed taxonomy. A hosted open-weight language model called over the network chooses among the supplied labels and explains the choice in a sentence or two; a label outside the supplied set is discarded. When that model does not answer within its time budget, everything below applies instead: a label wins on lexical relatedness, when a label word appears in the text or when text and label words are neighbours in the keyless Datamuse word index, and the answer names the words that matched so the choice can be checked. When no label clears the runner-up by a clear margin the text is reported as ambiguous between them rather than a label being guessed, and a negated label such as "not spam" is never chosen merely because evidence for the other is absent. Label sets of positive, negative and neutral are read with the sentiment word list instead. Where the word index does not respond, only direct label-word matches are counted and the answer says so; an ambiguity reached that way is reported as a source outage. Emotional tone on its own is SENTIMENT_ANALYSIS. A request without a label set or without text is refused by name.

Example questions: "Summarise the evidence on intermittent fasting and weight loss". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and sources. Findings on a topic gathered across several published studies and combined into one answer. PubMed and Europe PMC are searched on title and abstract, and from each study a single sentence reporting a result is quoted verbatim from its abstract and attributed by first author, year and PubMed id. A sentence is quoted only when it states a result, such as an association, a reduction or a conclusion, and when every topic word appears as a whole word in it or in the study's title. Statements of purpose ("To examine ..."), search and methods descriptions, definitions, background attributed to earlier work and calls for further research are never quoted as findings. Nothing is generated, and whether the studies agree is explicitly not assessed. Requests for the latest or recent studies are limited to the last five years. When the request supplies its own notes, on separate lines or run together on one line, they are restated grouped by source with their attributions kept, nothing is fetched, and a stated topic that no note addresses is named as unaddressed. Where only one study yields a quotable finding the answer says no synthesis across sources was possible; where both indexes fail that is reported as an outage and never as an absence of research. A cited answer to one narrow question is RESEARCH_QUERY rather than this intent.

Example questions: "Is it true that the Eiffel Tower is in Paris?", "Fact-check: water boils at 100 °C at sea level". Returns answer, verdict, confidence, reason, checked_at and claim, source, source_url, evidence. A specific claim, looked up against a citable encyclopaedic reference and reported with the article named and quoted. Reports an explicit refutation when the source states one, and otherwise says plainly that the source does not settle the claim. It does not adjudicate contested claims and never asserts that a claim is true on the strength of a topical match.

Screens a person, company or wallet against the OFAC SDN list and the UN Security Council Consolidated List, read live, including every listed alias and near-matches on spelling or transliteration. Example questions: "Screen 'Ivan Petrov, DOB 1974, Cyprus' against the OFAC SDN list", "Is Viktor But sanctioned?", "Is wallet 0x… on a sanctions list?". A birth year in the question is checked against the listed ones. Returns verdict (match, possible_match, no_match or unknown), confidence, matches (up to five, each with list, reference id, listed name, the name or alias that matched, type, programmes, score 0-1, listed birth years, whether the birth year agrees, nationalities, listing date and the OFAC record URL), closest (the nearest entry when nothing matched), lists_checked (each list with its published date and entry count) and lists_not_checked. The EU and UK lists are not screened and the answer says so. A name match alone never establishes identity, and the answer says that too.

A company's official register record, read live from the GLEIF LEI register and, for a US filer, SEC EDGAR. Example questions: "What is the incorporation status and registered agent for Tesla, Inc.?", "Is Barclays Bank PLC still registered?", "UK company number 01026167", "Look up LEI 5493001KJTIIGC8Y1R12". Returns verdict (found, not_found or unknown), legal_name, lei, entity_status (ACTIVE or INACTIVE), lei_registration_status, jurisdiction, legal_form, company_number and the register that issued it (Companies House, a US Secretary of State, …), registered_address, registered_agent when the registered address is an agent's, headquarters_address, incorporated, other_names, direct_parent and ultimate_parent (name and LEI), us_filer (CIK, state of incorporation, industry code, addresses and former names from EDGAR), other_candidates with similar names, and sources. Directors and beneficial owners are in neither source, and every answer says so instead of leaving them out silently.

Whether an issuer has filed a statutory filing on SEC EDGAR, when it was accepted, and what it reports, read live from the issuer's own EDGAR filing index. Example questions: "Has Tesla filed its latest 10-Q on SEC EDGAR, on what date was it accepted, and what did it disclose about margins?", "Did Apple file an 8-K in the last 30 days?", "What is Microsoft's most recent filing?". Covers 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, 20-F, 6-K, 40-F, S-1, DEF 14A and amendments. Returns verdict (filed, not_filed, not_found or unknown), company, cik, tickers, filing (form, filed date, EDGAR acceptance time in UTC, accession number, period or event date, 8-K items with their names, and the document URL), recent_filings (up to five), and for a 10-Q, 10-K or 20-F the figures tagged in that filing's XBRL: revenue, gross profit, gross margin, operating income and net income for its period, with prior_year_figures for the same period a year earlier. Only SEC EDGAR is read; a question about another regulator says that it is not covered.

Verifies one on-chain transfer by hash, read from public JSON-RPC on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, BNB Chain or Avalanche, with every chain searched when none is named. Example questions: "Verify transfer 0x…: did it succeed, who sent it to whom, how much fee was burned and how many confirmations does it have?". Returns verdict (confirmed, reverted, pending, not_found or unknown) and a transaction object with status, from, to, value_wei, value, symbol, block_number, block_hash, receipt_status, method, gas_used, fee_wei, confirmations, base_fee_wei and base_fee_burned: true on Ethereum and Polygon, where the EIP-1559 base fee is burned, false on rollups, where it is paid to the sequencer, and null before London or when the block could not be read. Confirmations are counted from the chain head at the time of the answer.

The latest released value of a macroeconomic statistic, read from the agency that publishes it. Example questions: "What was the latest US CPI year-over-year print, and what is the current federal funds target range?", "What is euro area inflation and the ECB deposit rate?", "What is the unemployment rate in Germany?", "What was Japan's GDP growth last year?". US CPI, core CPI and unemployment come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, monthly, with CPI computed year on year from the index; the federal funds target range and effective rate from the New York Fed, daily; euro area and EU inflation (HICP) and unemployment from Eurostat, monthly; ECB deposit and main refinancing rates from the ECB, daily; other countries' inflation, unemployment and GDP from the World Bank, annual and labelled annual. Returns verdict (reported, not_covered or unknown), region and indicators, each with value (and value_high for a range), unit, period, frequency, series id, source and source_url. Several statistics can be asked for at once. A policy rate outside the US and the euro area is named as not covered rather than replaced by another figure. A past year ("US inflation in 2023") returns that year's World Bank WDI annual value with its year, never the latest print.

Whether a URL or domain is listed as malicious, and by which sources, read live from two keyless threat sources: Cloudflare security DNS and Quad9 threat-blocking DNS, each compared with an unfiltered resolver, so a block is reported only for a name that really resolves. Example questions: "Check https://login-secure-update.example.com against threat feeds and DNS blocklists: is it listed for phishing, and by which engines?", "Is malware.testcategory.com on any blocklist?". Returns verdict, listed (true, false, or null when a source did not answer), sources (each with source, kind, and result listed, not_listed, unknown, unavailable or not_applicable), flagged_by, and the underlying checks: TLS certificate, lookalike markers, whether the host resolves, redirect count and final URL. A clean listing is never called proof of safety.

Answers an open-domain question, or a question about a passage supplied with it, with every factual claim cited to a numbered source. Example questions: "Who won the 2022 FIFA World Cup and where was it held?", "Why is the sky blue?", "Based on the following text: … When did the war end?". Open-domain sources are up to five English Wikipedia article introductions, found by searching the question, its keywords and its subject phrase; a supplied passage is the only source when one is given. A free model phrases the answer from those sources only, and the reply is kept only if every sentence cites a source that exists; otherwise the answer is the source sentence that best matches the question, quoted and cited. Returns verdict (answered, not_in_sources or unknown), method (model_phrased_from_sources or extracted_from_sources), and citations (number, title, URL and kind for each source). When the sources do not contain the answer it says so instead of guessing.

The DNS records a name publishes, read live from Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 and Google Public DNS over DNS-over-HTTPS and compared record by record. Example questions: "What are the MX records for github.com?", "What is the IPv6 address of google.com?", "Does paypal.com publish a DMARC record?". Record types A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA and CAA; a DMARC question is asked of _dmarc.<domain>, and A is used when no type is named. Returns verdict (resolved, no_records, nxdomain, resolvers_disagree or unknown), name, record_type, records, ttl, resolvers_agree, cname_chain, and resolvers (each with its status, records, TTL and DNSSEC-validated flag). A disagreement is reported with both sides, never resolved by picking one.

An ERC-20 token's total supply and burned balance, read with eth_call at one pinned block from two independent public RPCs and compared. Example questions: "What is the total supply of USDC on Ethereum?", "Verify the total supply and burned tokens of 0x95aD61b0a150d79219dCF64E1E6Cc01f0B64C4cE". Chains: Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism and Polygon; Ethereum when none is named. A symbol is resolved to its contract by DEX liquidity and refused as ambiguous when two contracts compete. Returns verdict (verified, providers_disagree, not_a_token, ambiguous, not_found or unknown), chain, token_address, symbol, decimals, total_supply (exact, in token units), total_supply_raw, burned and burned_raw (held at 0x…dEaD and the zero address), supply_net_of_burn, block_number, providers and providers_agree. Circulating supply is not computed, and the answer says so. No Solana SPL.

A direct reply to one message: general knowledge, reasoning, explanation or conversation, written by a language model. Example questions: "Why is the sky blue?", "Explain recursion to a ten-year-old", "Will it be possible to land humans on Mars by 2030?". Returns brief (the answer in one plain sentence of at most 80 characters), reply (the full answer, opening with that sentence), and verdict: Likely, Unlikely or Uncertain for a question about whether something will happen, answered otherwise. No model answer is verdict unknown with error upstream_unavailable, never an invented reply.

A review of supplied source code or a diff for correctness, security, performance and clarity. Example questions: "Review this function: <code>", "Is this SQL query safe? <code>". Returns verdict (Approve, Request changes or Comment; Request changes whenever a finding is critical or high, so a verdict never contradicts its own findings), summary (three to six sentences opening "The code is correct." or "The code is not correct.", then each serious issue explained), findings in severity order (each with severity critical, high, medium, low or info, line where known, the issue by its technical name and the concrete fix) and finding_count. Links are not fetched: send the code itself. Up to 8,000 characters.

A security audit of supplied Solidity source. Example questions: "Audit this contract: <code>", "Is this vault safe from reentrancy? <code>". Returns verdict (the overall risk grade: Critical, High, Medium, Low or No issues found, always the severity of the most serious finding), summary (prose that opens with that grade, then for each finding its class, function, severity, why it is exploitable and the concrete fix), findings in severity order (each with class: reentrancy, access control, unchecked external call, integer/precision, oracle manipulation, front-running, denial of service or upgradeability; function; severity; issue; fix) and finding_count. Links and addresses are not fetched: send the source itself. Up to 8,000 characters.

Free-form writing for a described task: drafting, rewriting, summarising, product copy, emails, outlines. Example questions: "Write a 60-word product description for a solar phone charger", "Rewrite this paragraph for a ten-year-old: <text>". Every stated constraint is honoured (length, format, tone, words to include), and the answer reports word_count next to requested_words so a length target can be checked. Returns text (the writing only, no preamble), title (always: a short title of at most eight words), brief (the text if at most 80 characters; for a multi-line text its first line when that fits; else its opening sentence cut to 80), word_count and requested_words.

One named value read from chain nodes at a stated block height or at "latest", with the block it was read at. Example questions: "At block 21000000 on ethereum, what amount did the Transfer log in tx 0x… carry, and how much gas did that tx use?", "What was USDC's total supply at block 21000000?", "How much ETH did 0x… hold at block 21000000?", "What is storage slot 0 of 0x… at block 21000000?", "How much gas did block 21000000 use?". Reads: a transaction receipt (gas used, status, fee and every ERC-20 or ERC-721 Transfer log), eth_getStorageAt, totalSupply(), a token's balanceOf() for a holder, the native balance, or a block's gas used, gas limit, base fee and transaction count. "latest" is pinned a few blocks behind the head so two providers read the same block. Every RPC of the chain is asked and the first two answers are compared; old state needs an archive node, so an answer read from one provider says so, and no answer is unknown, never zero. A block not yet produced is refused. Chains: Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon and BNB Chain; Ethereum when none is named. Returns verdict (verified, providers_disagree, not_found, insufficient_input or unknown), metric, block_number, block_anchor (stated or latest), value (exact, in token or coin units where they apply), value_raw, unit, providers, providers_agree, and for a transaction tx_hash, tx_status, gas_used, fee and transfers.

output_schema.description: /historical-prices returns {symbol | network+address, currency, data[]}. /prices-by-symbol and /prices-by-address return {data[]} where each item holds prices[] or an error string.

network.description: Present when requested by address, e.g. eth-mainnet.

symbol.description: Present when requested by symbol, e.g. ETH.

error.description: Present when this token's price is unavailable.

limitations.message: Free tier allows 300 requests per hour (Pay As You Go allows 10,000 per hour).
/prices-by-address accepts 1 to 25 addresses per request, spanning at most 3 networks.
With interval 5m, endTime minus startTime must not exceed 7 days.
With interval 1h, endTime minus startTime must not exceed 30 days.
With interval 1d, endTime minus startTime must not exceed 1 year.
/historical-prices returns one token per request, identified by a symbol or by a network plus address, never both.
Historic data is a single price per timestamp, not open/high/low/close candles.
Prices are quoted in USD only.

body.name: KoinMix Crypto Price Oracle
body.description: Multi-provider crypto spot price miner. Aggregates live quotes from independent market data providers (CoinGecko, CoinMarketCap, Binance, Coinbase) and emits a median-consensus price with an agreement-derived confidence score. The autonomous engine uses it for CRYPTO_PRICE intents: it returns a machine-readable signal carrying price, priceX1e8, confidence, sourceCount and spreadBps, and refuses rather than guessing when sources disagree beyond tolerance or all providers fail.
